text.p: Coffee futures defied analysts' expectations that they might take a respite from their blistering rally on Thursday and soared to 20-year highs on frantic buying from speculators.
Elsewhere on world commodity markets copper rose in value on the London Metal Exchange but gold suffered from reports of a likely revaluation of German bullion reserves.

New York precious metals ended higher, apart from palladium, as dealers puzzled over German announcements about the fate of yellow metal held in the mighty Bundesbank vaults. "The market reacted yesterday when it came out that they might sell some gold, a change of heart for the Germans. But Waigel made it clear they are not going to be selling any gold, just reevaluating it," Scott Mehlman, chief dealer at Credit Lyonnais Rouse said. German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Thursday not a single ounce of Bundesbank gold reserves would be sold and the country's reserves could be revalued. Gold prices dipped late Wednesday and overnight on fears, stemming from a newspaper article, that Germany might sell gold. COMEX June gold settled 20 cents firmer at $348.40 an ounce, traded $349.30 to $346.70 in largely choppy, erratic dealings. Bullion was at $347.20/$347.70 late afternoon.

COMEX copper ended near one year highs Thursday as the London market broke through key chart areas, triggering speculative buying and shortcovering amid falling stocks, good demand and labor concerns at key mines, dealers said. LME copper explored new upside territory in late inter-office trading, hitting a fresh one-year peak. At 1830 GMT, three month copper was quoted at $2,373/78 after trading as high as $2,483, up from a afternoon kerb close of $2,463, traders said. Buying on Comex helped lift prices above the $2,474 high seen in official activity. After the LME close, news came out that state copper worker in Chile would consider call strike action to protest against the government's report plans to privatise parts of the state oil company Enap and state metals smelting firm Enami.
The other metals were little changed.

A bullish wheat number in USDA's weekly export sales report plus signals the market was oversold boosted CBOT wheat futures to a higher close, traders said. U.S. net export sales of old and new crop wheat combined during the week ended May 8 totaled 705,500 tonnes, according to the USDA. That tally was above trade expectations for 350,000 to 500,000 tonnes. But many traders said the main reason for the firm close was the fact the market was oversold after the recent slide in the July contract to one month lows. Technical traders said the market was due for a bounce as the July nine day relative strength index early this week approached 30 percent. An RSI of 30 or less is viewed as an oversold market and an RSI of 70 or more is viewed as an overbought market. Support also may have come from firm cash basis markets and the U.S. Great Plains weather outlooks were for only scattered showers in the dry areas of western Kansas. Brent crude oil, the North Sea benchmark, slipped in late U.S. paper activity, traders said. A full boat of July Brent traded at $19.43 a barrel, down six cents from the settlement of London's IPE. Five partial July cargoes changed hands, three at $19.45 and two at $19.43 a barrel, traders said. Intermonth spreads were subdued. June/July was talked at minus one cent to flat, while July/August and August/September were each talked at minus three cents to flat, traders said.
